query: How can Singapore Airlines improve its overall rating and recommendation rate, especially on flights where passengers do not recommend it (Recommended = no)?

per_column.name: is_not_recommended
per_column.rationale: This is simply a binary re-encoding of the existing 'Recommended' field (the '(Recommended = no)' condition explicitly stated in the query). It is the outcome itself, not a cause; it cannot serve as treatment or confounder.

per_column.name: service_consistency_gap
per_column.rationale: A numeric gap derived from service-rating dimensions. It is a candidate driver (cause) of the overall rating, so it functions as a treatment/predictor, not as a common cause of a separate treatment and the outcome. It does not adjust for any prior variable.

per_column.name: has_critical_service_failure
per_column.rationale: A binary indicator of a service failure engineered from the service dimensions. This is exactly the kind of candidate cause whose effect on the rating one would attribute — a treatment, not a confounder.

per_column.name: poor_value_perception
per_column.rationale: Derived from 'Value For Money'; a rating driver / candidate cause of overall rating. It is a treatment (arguably even a mediator on the service→satisfaction path), but in no sense a common cause of another treatment and the outcome.

per_column.name: premium_with_low_rating
per_column.rationale: This interaction is defined partly on the OUTCOME itself ('low rating') combined with premium class. Conditioning on a variable built from the outcome opens collider bias; it is not a legitimate confounder (and would be an error to treat as one).

per_column.name: high_service_variance
per_column.rationale: A binary feature summarising dispersion across the service ratings — another engineered candidate cause of the overall rating. It is a treatment/predictor, not a common cause upstream of both a treatment and the outcome.

per_column.name: expectation_inflation
per_column.rationale: A signed gap between expected and delivered experience. This sits on the causal path (class/service → expectation gap → dissatisfaction/rating), i.e. a mediator, not a confounder. Adjusting for it as a confounder would be a mistake.

judge.rationale: A treatment is clearly present — indeed the system supplied several engineered candidate causes of low rating (critical service failure, poor value perception, service consistency gap, high service variance). But the decisive requirement is CONFOUNDERS: variables that plausibly cause BOTH one of these treatments AND the outcome and must be adjusted for. None of the added columns play that role. 'is_not_recommended' is the outcome; 'expectation_inflation' and 'poor_value_perception' are mediators/drivers on the causal path; and 'premium_with_low_rating' is built partly from the outcome, making it a collider rather than a confounder. The obvious real confounders for this problem (Type of Traveller, Class, Route/market, season/Month Flown) already exist in the base table, yet the augmentation surfaced NO new adjustment variable of that kind — no data/text-derived common cause was added. Because there are zero genuine, newly-surfaced confounders (confounder_quality 0.0), the columns set up prediction/feature engineering rather than an identifiable causal estimation, and the causal-attribution claim FAILS.
